structured_output.summary: Gaia RV scatter 14.5 km/s and 5σ secondary eclipse indicate a stellar companion.
reasons: Gaia radial velocities vary far beyond any planetary signal: gaia_rv_epoch_scatter_km_s 14.5, gaia_rv_epoch_range_km_s 47.9 over gaia_rv_nb_transits 15, gaia_rv_renormalised_gof 17.1, gaia_rv_chisq_pvalue 0.0, gaia_rv_variable True. A 4-day hot Jupiter would give a reflex amplitude of ~0.1-0.2 km/s; this scatter needs a companion of order a tenth of a solar mass, consistent with the pipeline's own gaia_rv_semi_amplitude_upper_limit_km_s 20.5 and gaia_rv_companion_mass_upper_limit_solar_masses 0.172 (an M dwarf, not a planet).

Gaia independently flags the star as a binary: gaia_non_single_star 2, i.e. a spectroscopic non-single-star solution (gaia_ruwe 1.08 shows it is not astrometric). Gaia does not produce spectroscopic binary solutions for planet-mass companions.

A secondary eclipse is detected at 5 sigma: secondary_depth_ppm 351 +/- secondary_depth_error_ppm 70, 4.5% of fit_depth_ppm 7737. Although below secondary_maximum_planet_depth_ppm 683 (so step 9 did not refute), a ~350 ppm eclipse is what a grazing late-M-dwarf companion on a stellar_radius_solar_radii 1.16 primary would give, and matches the RV-implied companion mass.

The transit geometry fits a grazing stellar eclipse: transit_grazing True, fit_impact_parameter 1.132 +/- 0.1592, fit_radius_ratio 0.2545 +/- 0.13613, V-shaped dips in all five sector panels of the all-sector figure, fit_duration_hours 1.693 for depth_ppm 6009-7737. A grazing 0.1-0.17 solar-mass companion reproduces depth, shape, secondary and RV together.

The signal is genuinely on the target, so the neighbour caution does not apply and this is not a blend: pixel_verdict on target in S38, S65, S101, S102 with joint_difference_image_snr 47.7 and joint_best_source TIC 331901355; the four pixel-check figures all centre the difference signal on the target pixel. That makes an on-target eclipsing binary, not a nearby one, the likely explanation.

Disagreement with the mechanical reasoning, not its outcome: the mechanical decision leads with planet_radius_earth_radii 32.24 above 22.4, but with a grazing transit the radius is almost unconstrained (planet_radius_error_earth_radii 17.25, fit_radius_ratio_error 0.136) and should not itself be grounds to drop. The drop rests on the Gaia RV variability, the Gaia non-single-star flag and the secondary eclipse.

TRICERATOPS does not rescue the candidate: triceratops_verdict likely planet with fpp_mean 0.2443 +/- fpp_standard_deviation 0.32 is far above validation thresholds and the model does not use the RV or secondary-eclipse evidence; nfpp_mean 0 only confirms the signal is on target.

Not held: released_tess_sectors_not_in_all_sector_verification and unreleased_tess_sectors_observing_the_star are both empty, and more TESS photometry would not change a case driven by Gaia radial velocities. Only multi-epoch RV follow-up could confirm the companion mass, which is outside this pipeline; exofop_tois, exofop_ctois and published_signal are empty, so the drop is on physical grounds, not duplication.

Minor supporting notes: odd_even_difference_sigma 2.35 and sector_depth_consistency_p_value 1.95e-12 (S38 8607 vs S101 6809 ppm) are mild inconsistencies, though cutout_sector_depth_consistency_p_value 0.235 suggests the sector scatter is largely aperture dilution; ellipsoidal_amplitude_ppm -267 +/- 388 is a non-detection consistent with a ~0.15 solar-mass companion at fit_scaled_semi_major_axis 9.92, so it neither supports nor contradicts the binary picture.
